summary: Mexico City is built on an ancient lakebed and due to human activity it is sinking. We added up a year of radar data from the NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite (27 consecutive interferograms, from Nov 11, 2025 to Oct 13, 2026, which is PROVISIONAL data) and built an open-source interactive web map of the Valley of Mexico. The radar data shows two sinking bowls one in the north-east (surrounding the airport and Nezahualcóyotl) and the south-east (surrounding Tláhuac and Chalco). At Nezahualcóyotl we found that the ground moved about 21.9 cm away from the satellite along the radar line of sight in 336 days. In Tláhuac we found a movement of about 16.4 cm. We estimate that about 3.2 million people (WorldPop 2020) live in our analysis area on ground moving faster than 10 cm per year along the line of sight. In Tláhuac, where one of us has family, the land sank so far that a new lake formed: water first pooled in 1988, and by 1991 it was a small lake. Our live app offers a six-step guided tour, radar images in HH and HV, a year of ground motion and seven landmark cards, so residents, students and decision makers can recognize and measure a hazard that is hard to see from the street.
details:
What our project does:
Project Lago is a free, interactive map of the Valley of Mexico built from a year of NISAR radar data. You can take a six-step guided tour or explore the valley on your own. You can easily switch between radar images and ground motion, swipe between dates, and open information cards for seven landmarks. Each card keeps what the radar data shows separate from what we infer and we make sure that we cite our sources.

The problem we had: 
Mexico City sits on an old lakebed and has been sinking for over a century, mainly because groundwater is pumped out and the clay beneath compacts from human development. This has caused issues such as The Angel of Independence needing 14 extra steps at its base as the ground has shifted. The sinking is too slow to see from the street, but cities need to know where it’s happening and how fast.

How our project works:
Our Python pipeline reads only the Mexico City slice of each NISAR file from NASA’s cloud, rather than downloading whole files. For ground motion we chained 27 back-to-back interferograms from Nov 11, 2025 to Oct 13, 2026. Every measurement is relative to a patch of hills on the west side that we assume is stable. Chaining cancels most of the atmospheric noise, and we confirmed the sign convention against NISAR’s own processing code and two standard radar tools. The site runs on Azure, with a backup on Cloudflare, and every change is tested before it goes live.

What we found:
Two sinking zones stand out. Around the airport and Nezahualcóyotl, the ground moved about 21.9 cm in 336 days which is roughly 2 cm a month. Around Tláhuac and Chalco it moved about 16.4 cm. The western hills barely moved. All figures are measured along the radar’s slanted line of sight, not straight down. Within our study area, roughly 3.2 million people (WorldPop 2020) live on ground sinking faster than 10 cm a year. Our results match NASA/JPL’s April 2026 NISAR image, which shows parts of the city sinking “more than 2 centimeters per month”.

The lake that came back story:
Lake Chalco was drained in the early 1900s to make space for farmland. As pumping made the ground sink, water collected in the new low spot again. These were initially small pools in 1988, but turned into a lake by 1991. We wanted to explore this story using the data as one of our teammates, Monica, has family from Santa Cecilia which is near Tláhuac. The radar shows that area is still sinking.

Limitations/shortcomings of our project:
The NISAR data is still provisional. Each number carries about 2 cm of uncertainty, and if the motion is purely vertical, true sinking is about 1.27 times our line-of-sight figures. We dropped three dates where the data looked wrong. NASA/JPL published this sinking first. What we add is an open, interactive tool with a full year of data and place-by-place numbers anyone can check.

What we want to do next:
Each new NISAR pass extends the record through the same pipeline. Next we’d like a Spanish version for residents, a second satellite track to separate vertical from sideways motion, and a screening map of where sinking ground and standing water overlap.

Our project was built with: TypeScript, React and MapLibre, Python, Azure static web app, Cloudflare, and github.
dataRefs: NASA/JPL: NISAR Maps Extreme Subsidence in Mexico City
